title: Even if all fall away (Mark 14:26–31)
hook: after a hymn, Peter swears he'll never desert him

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was covenant, a binding promise, in bread and cup in the upper room. Your line was take, this is my body.

The meal is over. Mark gives it one quiet line, in the King James Bible: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." A Passover meal traditionally closed with the psalms of praise called the Hallel, and those end with Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected, blessed is he that cometh. So they walk out singing, into the dark, across the valley, up the hill. On the way, Jesus says something that stops them. Tonight, all of you will fall away because of me. It is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Silence on the path. Then one voice, the one you'd expect, speaks up at once.
screen: `THEY SANG A HYMN.` → `OUT INTO THE DARK.` → `ALL OF YOU WILL FALL AWAY.`

segments.voice: Peter says: "Although all shall be offended, yet will not I." Even if everyone else falls away, not me. And he means it. He loves Jesus, and he believes he's strong enough. Jesus answers with painful precision: "this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice." Only Mark has the rooster crow twice. Peter doubles down, louder: "If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise." Then Mark adds five small, devastating words: "Likewise also said they all." The word the King James translates offended is skandalizō in Greek. It comes from a skandalon, the trigger stick of a trap, the thing that trips you. It's where English gets the word scandal. So falling away isn't a slow drift. It's getting caught, suddenly, by something you didn't see. And here's the part almost everyone skips. Between the warning and Peter's boast, Jesus slips in a promise: "But after that I am risen, I will go before you into Galilee." Before they've failed, he's already arranged to meet them afterward. The shepherd will be struck, the sheep will scatter, and the shepherd will go ahead of them to gather them again. Christians have found great comfort in that order: the failure foreseen, the meeting planned first. Peter's courage is real, and it isn't enough. What holds is not his promise to Jesus, but Jesus's promise to him.
screen: `YET WILL NOT I.` · `THE COCK WILL CROW TWICE.` · `SKANDALON: THE TRIGGER OF A TRAP.` · `I WILL GO BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.` · then, large: `LIKEWISE ALSO SAID THEY ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've promised, to yourself or someone else, with total confidence: I'll never snap at the kids again, I'll definitely stay calm, I'd never do that. Hold it gently, and instead of doubling down, try saying: I want to, and I may not manage it; notice whether that feels weaker, or truer. If you pray, ask for help rather than promising strength.
Skandalon, the trigger stick of a trap, a stumbling block. Peter's promise: not me. Sincere, and not strong enough.
Your line: not I, said Peter. But Galilee was planned first. That's day two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many Christians remember Peter's boast and later failure in Holy Week services, and they often point to him as a sign that God keeps faith with people who overestimate their own strength.
